sections.heading: Dialogue II, Knot viii, part 1 (printed pp. 201–208)
rows: [p. 201] Ereu. Habes Galilaei systema, illic argumenta ista & convoluta & evoluta leges. [Margin: Nodus VIII. Aerem usque [p. 202] ad confinia lunae a terra circumferri.] Vin'tu ut huic Asphalio occinam quae suis non minus digitis expedita habet.

[p. 201] Ereu. You have Galileo's system; there you will read those arguments both rolled up and unrolled [convoluta & evoluta]. [Margin: Knot VIII. That the air as far as [p. 202] the borders of the moon is carried round by the earth [terra].] Do you want that I should sing over [occinam] to this Asphalius things which he has ready [expedita] no less at his own fingers [digitis]?

Andab. Si nil apud te valeat praeter Galilaeum, ipsomet usus pro telo ad te depugno. Novisti itaque ipsum asserere & in Pacifico mari, & super montium cacumina, aerem non aeque cum terra volutari, & denique in causa aestus ipsam aquam minus obedientem telluri agnoscere. Immo ipse tu aquam quam ponis causam motus telluris, non eam tamen cursu assequi contendis. Ex his itaque duabus tibi sacris authoritatibus, quin & ipsa ratione sic depugno. Universim corpora rariora non aeque retinendi motus capacia sunt quam corpora densa. Neque aqua itaque, neque nubes, neque crepuscula, neque Aquilae circa summas Alpes evolantes sequi poterunt vim telluris orbita circumlatae diurna, nedum annua. Omnia ergo haec retrorsus contra motum terrae ferri videbuntur, si tellus moveri ponatur.

Andab. If nothing avails with you except Galileo, using [him] himself for a weapon I fight it out [depugno] against you. You know therefore that he himself asserts that both in the Pacific sea and above the summits of the mountains the air is not equally rolled round with the earth [terra], and finally, in the cause of the tide [aestus], acknowledges the water itself [to be] less obedient to the earth [telluri]. Nay, you yourself, the water which you put [as] cause of the motion of the earth [telluris], yet you contend that it does not keep up with it in [its] course. From these two authorities, therefore, sacred to you, nay and from reason [ratione] itself, I fight it out thus. Universally [Universim] rarer bodies are not equally capable of retaining motion as dense bodies. Therefore neither water, nor clouds, nor twilights [crepuscula], nor Eagles flying out about the highest Alps will be able to follow the force [vim] of the earth [telluris] carried round in the diurnal orbit, much less [nedum] the annual. All these things therefore will be seen to be borne backwards against the motion of the earth [terrae], if the earth [tellus] be supposed [ponatur] to be moved.

Ereu. Strenue, Andabata, sed quoniam in his quae motum efficiunt aliquantulum a Galilaeo diversus incedo, cogor ea breviter statuere principia quibus ad horum solutionem mihi utendum est. Meministi itaque, Andabata, hoc inter nos hesterna die constitutum, Nihil nihil esse: seu spatii imaginarii nullas esse partes; ipsumque ad loci motusque rationem nihil omnino posse conducere: quoniam quod ad realem & existentem effectum confert, ipsum etiam reale esse & existere [p. 203] necessum est. Ex hoc tua (ut autumo) pace infero, nihil motui locali resistere posse, & nihil ab eo pertransiri, nisi verum & reale corpus. Et quoniam primae differentiae corporis seu quanti sunt esse rarum & densum, seu magis & minus quantum vel divisibile, seu plus habere de substantia minus de quantitate, vel e diverso (haec enim omnia idem sunt) fit omne resistens motui vel divisum per motum & per transitum a mobili, esse in aliquo determinato gradu raritatis & densitatis, seu habere determinatam resistentiam ad hoc ut dividatur ab ipso mobili. Habesne aliquid quod circa haec dicta molestiam tibi creet? an tam evidentia & clara sunt quam solem medio die lucere?

Ereu. Vigorously [done], Andabata; but since in those things which effect motion I step [incedo] a little different from Galileo, I am compelled briefly to establish those principles which I must use for the solution of these [things]. You remember therefore, Andabata, this [was] settled between us on yesterday's day: that Nothing is nothing: or that of imaginary space [spatii imaginarii] there are no parts; and that it itself can contribute nothing at all to the reason [rationem] of place and motion: since what contributes to a real and existing effect, that itself also must [p. 203] needs [necessum est] be real and exist. From this, by your leave [tua pace] (as I reckon [autumo]), I infer that nothing can resist local motion, and nothing be passed through by it, except a true and real body. And since the first differences of body or of a quantum [quanti] are to be rare and dense, or more and less quantum or divisible, or to have more of substance [substantia], less of quantity, or the reverse (for all these are the same), it comes about [fit] that everything resisting motion, or divided by the motion and by the passage [transitum] of the mobile, is in some determinate degree of rarity and density, or has a determinate resistance to this, that it be divided by the mobile itself. Have you anything which creates trouble for you about these things said? or are they as evident and clear as that the sun shines at mid-day?
Andab. Hactenus nihil mysterii elocutus es, sunt enim ut dixisti Zenithio sole illustriora.
Andab. So far you have spoken out nothing of mystery; for they are, as you said, clearer [illustriora] than the Zenith [Zenithio] sun.

Ereu. Ex his conficio nullam esse resistentiam ad motum in ullo mobili, nisi ubi aliquis est cum alio corpore conflictus & oppositio: quod ipsum cum de telluris agitatione ageremus, semel aut iterum confessus es, postquam de magnitudine & gravitate opposuisses. Haeccine meministi? & adhuc tibi constas? vel [p. 204] si minus tibi constas, cogita rursus quid in ipso corpore motui possit obsistere, praeter extrinsecum resistens ad divisionem seu impediens transitum corpori.

Ereu. From these I gather [conficio] that there is no resistance to motion in any mobile, except where there is some conflict and opposition with another body: which very thing, when we were treating of the agitation of the earth [telluris], you confessed once or again, after you had objected [opposuisses] about magnitude and heaviness [gravitate]. Do you remember these things? and are you still consistent with yourself [tibi constas]? or [p. 204] if you are less consistent with yourself, consider again what in the body itself could stand against [obsistere] motion, besides an extrinsic [thing] resisting division or impeding passage to the body.
Andab. Quam ipse suggessisti gravitas, & qui tantumdem valet impetus in quamlibet aliam partem.
Andab. [That is,] heaviness [gravitas], which you yourself suggested, and impetus, which avails just as much towards any other part [partem] whatever.

Ereu. Tu doces quomodo motus motui sit oppositus, nos vero quomodo corpus motui sit oppositum indagamus. Hoc itaque concessum accipio, corpus non alia motum, aliam oppositionem ad motum non habere, quam resistentiam, quam vocant medii seu corporis ambientis, quod scindit vel pellit ut moveatur. Et nunc terram contemplare, & aerem quem ei circumpositum vides, quem ad lunae usque confinia sese extendere ab hesterna disputatione accipiemus: illic enim, si memini, definitum est aerem non esse aliud quam evaporatum ex singulis corporibus crassioribus liquorem, & suum esse cuique Astro congeneum. Quare necesse est Astra maiora maiorem quoque vaporum sphaeram habere, & in proportione corporum & exhalabilitatis determinatam esse copiam & limites planetarum nostrorum. Et secundum haec aer quem expirat nostra tellus, eo se extendere debet, donec lunaribus effluviis commisceatur. Orbem itaque hunc magnum ex tellure mari & [p. 205] aere contuere. Et quoniam omne corpus, ut diximus, determinatum gradum raritatis & densitatis habet, aliquam oppositionem necessario habebit aer, & tanto maiorem quanto telluri propinquior est, eo enim spissior & aquai propior est, & ab omnibus habetur. Accedit ad haec insita gravitas & conatus ad centrum pro suo posse, quem sicut in corporibus densis oculis ipsis perspicimus, sic in aere quoque intelligimus solidare partes ipsius versus terram. Haeccine prout exposita sunt placent tibi, Andabata, an in aliquo offendi?

Ereu. You teach how motion is opposed to motion, but we are tracking out [indagamus] how body is opposed to motion. This therefore I take [as] granted, that a body not otherwise moved [non alia motum] has no other opposition to motion than the resistance which they call [that] of the medium [medii] or of the surrounding body, which it cuts or drives in order that it be moved. And now contemplate the earth [terram], and the air which you see placed round it, which we shall accept from yesterday's disputation to extend itself as far as the borders of the moon: for there, if I remember, it was defined that air is not anything other than a liquor [liquorem] evaporated from the several grosser bodies, and that to each Star [Astro] its own [air] is congeneous [congeneum]. Wherefore it is necessary that greater Stars have also a greater sphere of vapours, and that in proportion of the bodies and of exhalability [exhalabilitatis] the quantity [copiam] and limits of our planets are determinate. And according to these things the air which our earth [tellus] breathes out must extend itself thither, until it is mixed together with the lunar effluvia. Behold [contuere] therefore this great orb [made up] of earth [tellure], sea and [p. 205] air. And since every body, as we have said, has a determinate degree of rarity and density, the air will necessarily have some opposition, and so much the greater as it is nearer to the earth [telluri]; for there it is thicker [spissior] and nearer to water [aquai], and is [so] held by all. There is added to these the implanted heaviness [gravitas] and endeavour [conatus] to the centre according to its power [pro suo posse], which, as in dense bodies we perceive with the eyes themselves, so in the air also we understand to solidify [solidare] its parts towards the earth [terram]. Do these things, as they have been set forth, please you, Andabata, or have I offended in anything?
Andab. De ceteris non laboro, sed quod novissime de gravitate aeris dixisti, non adeo arridet. Aerem enim in ipso aere gravitare neque rationi, neque experientiae mihi consonum videtur.

Andab. About the rest I am not troubled [non laboro]; but what you said most recently about the heaviness of air does not much smile on [me] [non adeo arridet]. For that air gravitates [gravitare] in air itself seems to me consonant neither with reason [rationi] nor with experience.

Ereu. Non male dixisti. Aerem enim aeri cum comparamus, aequalem aequali comparare intendimus, quomodo clarum est unum alteri non praeponderare. Sed si graviorem alium alio faciamus, necesse est sua quemque proportione ad terram ferri. Et hoc nosti quoad aeris regiones in propatulo esse, neque quoad singulas regionum partes multum esse disputabile. Certe in aqua tam periti sumus, ut in qua parte aquae velimus, molem quae demersa ad eam partem emergat, emersa ipsam [p. 206] se in eandem devergat, conficere possimus. Non ego, Andabata, sed qui similibus animum & manus adiiciunt. Ex his itaque hoc statutum maneat, aerem totum suis gradibus ad tellurem & centrum niti, perque hunc conatum, pro suo modulo, haerere & defigi. His itaque compositis, fac tellurem cui aer haereat, moveri, fac aerem continuum usque ad lunares afflatus, ita ut ubi illis primo miscetur, tenuissimus sit, & ex iis quae iam vera esse inter nos statuimus, elice quid aere futurum sit.

Ereu. You have not spoken ill. For when we compare air to air, we intend to compare equal to equal, in which way it is clear that one does not outweigh [praeponderare] the other. But if we make one heavier than another, it is necessary that each be borne to the earth [terram] in its own proportion. And this you know to be in the open [in propatulo] as regards the regions of the air, and as regards the single parts of the regions not to be much disputable. Certainly in water we are so skilled that in whatever part of the water we wish, we can make [conficere] a mass which, sunk, would emerge to that part, [and] having emerged, would [p. 206] incline itself down [devergat] into the same. Not I, Andabata, but those who apply mind and hands to similar things. From these therefore let this remain established: that the whole air by its degrees strives [niti] to the earth [tellurem] and the centre, and through this endeavour [conatum], according to its little measure [pro suo modulo], clings and is fixed down [haerere & defigi]. These things therefore being put together [compositis], make [fac] the earth [tellurem], to which the air clings, be moved; make the air continuous as far as the lunar breathings [afflatus], so that where it is first mixed with them it is most thin [tenuissimus]; and from those things which we have now established between us to be true, draw out [elice] what will become of the air.

Andab. Si ex dictis tuis gradus mihi faciendi sunt, haec video esse {?causa} aeri cur a tellure non distrahatur, gravitatem scilicet & eam adhaerescentiam qua sicco agglutinantur humentia. Cur autem resistat motui nullam causam video donec ad terminos terrestrium & lunarium effluviorum perventum sit: ibi autem tenuissima utraque video, hoc est, facillima divisu. Clarum est itaque ex hoc discursu ibi magis divisionem futuram quam prope tellurem. Totus itaque hic aer circumferetur cum terra, & quidem quantum ipsa tellus. Aies enim quoties dixero alicubi resistere, quae causa est in tantum obsistens motui, ut nexum inter ipsum & tellurem abrumpere possit? quam ut inveniam, haerebo. Ex tuis itaque verbis hoc sequi video. Non [p. 207] tamen persuasum mihi credas. Quantumvis enim fatear me non habere quod deductioni tuae extemporaneus opponam, res tamen ipsa tantum me sua paradoxa specie percellit, ut fidem adiicere non valeam. Quomodo enim vis ut credam tam lubricum & scissile elementum vehementem illum telluris cursum consectari posse?

Andab. If from your sayings steps [gradus] are to be made by me, these I see to be the cause[s] [causa] for the air why it is not drawn apart from the earth [tellure]: namely heaviness [gravitatem], and that adhesiveness [adhaerescentiam] by which moist things are glued to the dry. But why it should resist motion I see no cause, until one has come to the limits [terminos] of the terrestrial and lunar effluvia: but there I see both most thin, that is, most easy to divide. It is clear therefore from this discourse [discursu] that division will be [future] more there than near the earth [tellurem]. This whole air therefore will be carried round with the earth [terra], and indeed as much as the earth [tellus] itself. For you will say [Aies], as often as I shall have said that it resists somewhere: what cause is there resisting motion so far [in tantum] as to be able to break off the bond between it and the earth [tellurem]? which, that I may find it, I shall stick fast [haerebo]. From your words therefore I see this to follow. Yet [p. 207] do not believe me persuaded. For however much I confess I have not anything which I might oppose extempore to your deduction [deductioni], yet the thing itself so strikes me down [percellit] with its paradoxical appearance [specie] that I am not able to add [adiicere] belief. For how do you want me to believe that so slippery and splittable [scissile] an element can pursue [consectari] that vehement course of the earth [telluris]?

Ereu. Vidistine aliquando curru vectum qui fugam ipsius currus non valeret assequi? aut navi vectus sensisti quanta celeritate fluctus praetervolares? aut dum hac ipsa terra pedibus nixi haeremus, motum ipsius tam velocem quomodo assequaris laboras? Cogita itaque aerem sua gravitate in se hoc perficere, quod nobis sessio in curru, vel statio in terra addit. Unde vehitur aer tellure, neque ad sequendum allaborat, vel proprio nisu contendit.

Ereu. Have you ever seen [one] carried in a chariot [curru] who was not able to keep up with the flight of the chariot itself? or, carried in a ship, have you felt with how much speed you were flying past [praetervolares] the waves? or, while we cling to this very earth [terra], leaning [nixi] on our feet, do you labour how you may keep up with its so swift motion? Consider therefore that the air by its own heaviness [gravitate] accomplishes this in itself, which the sitting [sessio] in the chariot, or standing [statio] on the earth [terra], adds to us. Whence the air is carried by the earth [tellure], and neither labours to follow, nor strives by its own effort [nisu].

Andab. Effunde quantumvis elegantium exemplorum. Ego me in Thomarum familiam ab hac hora coopto, addico, consecro. Nisi experimenta mihi sensibus obnoxia attuleris, nihil fucatae tuae orationi credo: fallaces sunt omnes deductiones tuae & nihil assentior.

Andab. Pour out as many elegant examples as you like [quantumvis]. I from this hour co-opt, make over [addico], [and] consecrate myself into the family of the Thomases. Unless you bring me experiments [experimenta] subject [obnoxia] to the senses, I believe nothing to your painted [fucatae] speech: deceitful are all your deductions, and I assent to nothing.

Asphal. Meminisse oportet materiei quam tractamus, de aere esse sermonem, quem praesentem & circumstantem videre non valemus, [p. 208] & solo discursu percipimus, pluribus inane merum & aestimantibus & appellantibus: & tu petis experimenta ex iis locis ad quae vix oculis pertingimus. Non est ex ratione quod agis; accommodatas oportet ad materiei naturam expectare argumentationes.

Asphal. One ought to remember of the matter [materiei] which we treat that the conversation [sermonem] is about air, which, [though] present and standing round [us], we are not able to see, [p. 208] and perceive by discourse [discursu] alone, very many both esteeming and calling [it] mere void [inane merum]: and you seek experiments from those places to which we scarcely reach with the eyes. What you do is not according to reason [ex ratione]; one ought to expect argumentations accommodated to the nature of the matter [materiei].
Andab. Etiam Brutum me & stipitem existima, Asphali, sis. Ego interea non decedo verbis meis; nisi videro, non credam.
Andab. Think me even a Brute [Brutum] and a stock [stipitem], Asphalius, if you please [sis]. I meanwhile do not depart from my words: unless I see, I shall not believe.

terms: involved and developed; stated compactly and then unfolded; possibly ‘wound in and wound out’ of the argument.
Image of a book-roll (volumen): Galileo's Dialogo states the objections and then unrolls their answers (Day II on air, clouds and birds).
to sing to, chant in reply; also of ill-omened birds ‘to croak’.
Ironic: Ereunius would only be ‘chanting’ to Asphalius what he already knows.
ad digitos / in digitis expeditum habere
to have at one's fingertips, know thoroughly.
Andabata's martial persona (andabatae were blindfolded gladiators).
twilight; here the twilight vapours/haze high in the atmosphere (cf. ‘nebulas crepusculinas’, p. 208).
Early-modern astronomers estimated the height of the twilight-making atmosphere (c. 50 miles, as p. 208 says).
still less, not to speak of.
Comparative force; diurnal vs annual motion.
the non-existent has no properties; nothing is not something.
Digbean/Whitean rejection of real imaginary space (cf. D1, and spatium imaginarium in glossary).
with your peace, with your permission.
the first differences of body or of a quantum
Digby's (and White's) doctrine that rare and dense are the primary differences of quantity, defined as more or less divisible, or more substance under less quantity (Two Treatises, I.3).
to remain consistent, stand by oneself.
the medium through which motion occurs.
Aristotelian resistance of the medium; White reduces all resistance to it.
possibly ‘not moved by another [motion]’; or a misprint.
Each star has its own atmosphere of its own kind (D1 doctrine of effluvia).
pro suo posse / pro suo modulo
according to its power / according to its little measure
as far as it can / in its small proportion.
Scholastic ‘pro posse’; modulus = diminutive of modus.
Gravity compacting the parts of air downward.
to weigh, press down by weight.
Late Latin; the question whether air has weight ‘in its own place’ (Aristotle De caelo IV.4; cf. Galileo, Two New Sciences).
A body of neutral buoyancy at a chosen depth (hydrostatic balancing).
to proceed step by step (in argument).
Moist bodies glued to dry: White's account of cohesion (D1).
be at a loss, be stuck.
Pun on haerere used of air clinging to the earth.
Contrast with the rare/dense doctrine of divisibility.
Biblical allusion; Andabata's ‘nisi videro, non credam’ at the end echoes Thomas the apostle.
The vulgar opinion that air is nothing; Lucretian ‘inane’.
a dumb beast and a log (blockhead).
notes: Unit: Dialogue II, Knot viii, part 1 of 2. PDF pp. 212–219 = printed pp. 201–208, from ‘Ereu. Habes Galilaei systema’ (p. 201, beside the marginal ‘Nodus VIII. Aerem usque ad confinia lunae a terra circumferri’, running onto p. 202) to Andabata's ‘…nisi videro, non credam’ (p. 208). Part 2 begins on p. 208 with ‘Ereu. Andabatae quatenus possumus, gerendus est mos’, beside the marginal ‘Phaenomena motum aeris testantia’, and runs to the start of knot ix on p. 212 (PDF 223, marginal ‘Nodus IX. Corpus loco moveri’, beside ‘Ereu. Permitte ut paulo altius rem incipiam’).
Offset +11 holds (running heads 201–208; signatures Cc p. 201, Cc ij p. 203, Cc iij p. 205).

Uncertain or noted readings: (1) p. 201/202 ‘Vin'’ (end of p. 201) + ‘tu ut’ (start of p. 202) joined as ‘Vin'tu ut’; the sentence lacks a printed question mark and is translated as a question. (2) p. 204 ‘corpus non aliâ motum, aliam oppositionem’ — construction doubtful: either ‘a body not otherwise moved’ (i.e. without any other motion acting on it) or a compositor's doublet for ‘corpus non aliam oppositionem’; translated as printed. (3) p. 206 ‘haec video esse causá aëri’ (checked on a 300-dpi crop: accented final a) — an ablative does not construe in the accusative-and-infinitive; ‘causas’ (agreeing with haec … gravitatem … adhaerescentiam) is probably meant; transcribed {?causa} and translated ‘cause[s]’. (4) p. 205 ‘aquaï’ kept as the archaic genitive ‘aquai’. (5) p. 207 ‘Quantumuis … opponam ,’ — a wide gap before the comma in the print, nothing missing. (6) The marginal title runs across the page break (p. 201 ‘Aerem ysque’, p. 202 ‘ad confinia lunae a terra circumferri’).

Verification pass: each Latin sentence was re-read against the page images (150 dpi, with 300-dpi crops of p. 204 ‘aliâ motum’ and p. 206 ‘causá’) and against the English; nothing found omitted or added. 3 corrections: (1) ‘quanta celeritate fluctus praetervolares’ — imperfect subjunctive in indirect question rendered ‘you were flying past’ (draft: ‘you would fly past’); (2) ‘causá’ re-read from the crop and construed as plural ‘causes’ (draft: ‘the cause’); (3) ‘quoties dixero’ — future perfect rendered ‘as often as I shall have said’ (draft: ‘as often as I say’).

Conventions: as in the glossary — tellus ‘earth [tellus]’ and terra ‘earth [terra]’ bracketed throughout; supplied words in square brackets; page breaks marked [p. n] inside the row where they fall; ‘gravitas’ rendered ‘heaviness’ as before.
